slides.title: Engineering practice and automation
slides.thesis: Every technique must discharge a named verification claim.
notes: Open with a decision the audience must make in this area. Ask which result they currently treat as sufficient evidence and keep that answer for the closing discussion.
The lesson selects a practical argument from the book. The study handout preserves the detailed examples, citations and worked artifacts.

slides.title: Learning outcomes
slides.thesis: Demonstrate these decisions on a real plan row.
bullets: Assign ownership across verification handoffs.
Interpret an ML result by task and denominator.
Admit generated checkers through accountable review.
Choose an improvement from the local verification bottleneck.
notes: Read the outcomes as observable tasks. Ask learners to identify which one they can already demonstrate and which one currently depends on undocumented judgment.
At closure, require a concrete artifact or explanation for an outcome rather than a general expression of confidence.

slides.title: Route through the lesson
slides.thesis: Four blocks, each ending with a decision.
bullets: Make responsibilities observable
Read machine-learning evidence
Keep accountable human gates
Choose the next improvement
notes: Allow eighteen minutes for each block: a concept, its engineering consequence, a worked interpretation and a short discussion. Keep the discussion tied to the evidence available in the example.
Reserve the final eleven minutes for the assigned exercise and application to the learners’ work. The timing is a course design allocation, not an engineering estimate.

slides.title: An artifact owner is not the whole outcome
slides.thesis: Integration seams need explicit responsibility.
bullets: Name who resolves cross-team discrepancies.
Keep the expected evidence visible at handoff.
notes: Use a checker and model owned by different teams. Both can be delivered while their disagreement remains unresolved.
Assign responsibility for the outcome, including the interface between artifacts. The owner should be able to say which evidence permits the receiving team to proceed.

slides.title: Reviews answer different questions
slides.thesis: Plan, code and closure reviews need different inputs.
notes: Ask which review detects a missing requirement, which challenges a checker implementation and which accepts residual risk. Treating them as one generic approval loses those distinctions.
Bring the artifact that makes each question answerable. A coverage dashboard does not replace the specification at a plan review, and a code review does not authorize a waiver.

slides.title: Reproduction is an onboarding milestone
slides.thesis: A newcomer should establish evidence before explaining architecture.
bullets: Start from a known failure and its reproducer.
Produce a useful bug report and trace the ownership path.
notes: A guided defect teaches the actual run environment, observations and team interfaces. Ask the newcomer to reproduce it without depending on an undocumented working directory.
Judge onboarding by a small useful artifact rather than vocabulary recall. The exercise also exposes missing process documentation in the team.

slides.title: Discussion: every deliverable has an owner
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: The model and checker were both delivered.
Their disagreement blocks integration.
Which responsibility was left unnamed?
notes: Expected answer: responsibility for resolving the combined verification outcome at the seam, including authority to settle intent.
Ask learners to define the evidence and escalation path that make the handoff complete. Merely adding another status meeting does not resolve ownership.

slides.title: Evaluate the proposed operational use
slides.thesis: A measured task outcome is more useful than generic accuracy.
bullets: Use held-back data and a relevant comparison.
Re-measure when the design or failure population changes.
notes: Use the chapter’s triage-classifier proposal. Agreement with the human triage decisions measures the task the classifier is being proposed to assist, within that held-back population.
A changed design or failure distribution can invalidate the estimate. Keep an owner, monitoring cadence and retraining cost with the deployment decision.

slides.title: A benchmark needs its denominator
slides.thesis: Artifact class and acceptance criterion determine the meaning.
bullets: Record filtering and excluded cases.
Compare like tasks before comparing headline results.
notes: The chapter compares studies producing different artifacts under different criteria. Ask what was counted as successful, what humans filtered, and what target set remained.
A result on one protocol or design does not establish a trend across workflows. Describe the reported experiment precisely before drawing a transfer claim for the local project.

slides.title: A generated checker can become a bad oracle
slides.thesis: A proof against current RTL does not establish intended behavior.
bullets: Inspect timing direction and activation.
Challenge both design and generated interpretation.
notes: A syntactically valid property may express the wrong temporal relation or never activate. A proof against the current design can confirm consistency while preserving the original intent error.
Ask what independent observation would reject the plausible but wrong property. Mechanical checking reduces the candidate set; it does not remove the need to inspect the intended claim.

slides.title: Discussion: most generated properties prove
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: Generated properties pass against the current RTL.
No one has checked them against intent.
What has the reported result established?
notes: Expected answer: consistency with that design under the proof environment, for the properties and candidates included in the measurement.
It has not established that the properties express the intended behavior or cover all required plan rows. Ask which acceptance work is still owed.

slides.title: Filter mechanically before intent review
slides.thesis: Human attention should reach candidates with a clear provenance.
notes: Use parsing, elaboration, signal resolution and available semantic checks to remove mechanical failures before asking a reviewer to assess intent.
The reviewer still decides whether the surviving property expresses the requirement and is admitted into the plan. A tool pass must not silently perform that admission.

slides.title: Correlated errors defeat casual sampling
slides.thesis: A shared generation mistake can affect an entire batch.
bullets: Inspect systematic translation risks.
Do not infer batch correctness from a few plausible examples.
notes: Explain why repeated use of the same flawed template or interpretation creates dependent errors. A small informal sample does not establish the reliability of the unreviewed remainder.
Choose review and validation according to the artifact’s role as an oracle. The chapter keeps acceptance authority with the people responsible for the verification claim.

slides.title: Preserve the accepted artifact, not just the model name
slides.thesis: Provenance must support reconstruction of the decision.
bullets: Retain relevant inputs, generated text and accepted revision.
Record reviewer, rationale and applicable restrictions.
notes: A model identifier does not identify the prompt context, retrieved specification, generation or human edits that produced the checker in use.
Keep the actual accepted artifact and the evidence supporting admission. Apply the project’s data-handling rules to the inputs and outputs before using the workflow.

slides.title: Discussion: approval of a sampled batch
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: A reviewer checks a few generated properties.
All share the same translation template.
What uncertainty remains about the batch?
notes: Expected answer: a systematic error in the shared template or interpretation can affect many unreviewed properties. The sample’s plausibility does not establish their intent correctness.
Ask for a validation action targeted at that shared failure mode and a traceable acceptance decision for the artifacts actually admitted.

slides.title: The bottleneck depends on the project level
slides.thesis: A block and a software workload can need different improvements.
bullets: Separate knowing what to check from execution capacity.
Measure the local constraint before investing.
notes: Contrast a block regression that already fits overnight with a system workload that cannot reach its useful software state in time. More execution capacity addresses only one of those immediate constraints.
The chapter’s claim is conditional on level and workload. Do not turn it into a universal prediction about every verification team.

slides.title: Earlier and later evidence are complementary
slides.thesis: Moving a check does not erase its original scope obligations.
bullets: Use early models with explicit fidelity limits.
Retain deep block checking alongside system execution.
notes: Earlier models expose integration or software problems before RTL is ready; later platforms exercise behaviors that need long execution or physical observations.
Neither movement justifies dropping a plan row without replacement evidence for the same claim. Review the handoff of model assumptions and residual behavior.

slides.title: Automation moves work without removing judgment
slides.thesis: Partial oracles and model boundaries remain engineering problems.
bullets: Improve the weakest evidence-producing step.
Keep interpretation, review and ownership explicit.
notes: Separate contingent tool capacity from durable limitations such as incomplete specifications and partial observation. Better automation can change the cost of a task without deciding what correctness should mean.
Ask learners to name a proposed improvement and the claim it strengthens. This keeps future-looking discussion tied to an inspectable engineering outcome.

slides.title: Discussion: cut regression after a new proof
slides.thesis: Name the evidence that would settle the decision.
bullets: A new formal result motivates removing simulation work.
Its model covers only part of the old claim.
What evidence is required before the cut?
notes: Expected answer: show that the retained and replacement evidence jointly discharge the original plan row, including behavior outside the proof model.
A proof’s strength does not make it transferable to an unrelated boundary. Preserve the residual simulation obligation or explicitly revise the claim with a reviewed risk decision.

slides.title: Exercise: compare two automation proposals
slides.thesis: Distinguish task evidence from design consistency.
bullets: One classifier is measured against held-back human triage.
Generated properties instead prove against current RTL.
Explain which result measures its proposed use and what remains unknown.
notes: Assign book Exercise 25.2 in full. Use the chapter’s stated held-back comparison without treating its illustrative result as a prediction for another project.

Expected answer: the classifier measurement evaluates the proposed operational task against independent human triage on held-back history. Passing proofs show consistency with the modeled RTL and assumptions; they do not establish that generated properties express the intended specification.

slides.title: What to change on Monday
slides.thesis: Make one existing verification decision reviewable.
bullets: Repair one unowned integration handoff.
Audit provenance for an accepted generated checker.
Measure the bottleneck before selecting an automation project.
notes: Ask each learner to choose one of these actions in an existing project. Require a small, inspectable deliverable and identify the person who will review it.
Keep the change connected to the lesson’s evidence limits. A new dashboard, script or model is useful only if it strengthens the claim the plan row is meant to establish.

slides.title: Scope and next reading
slides.thesis: Use the handout for the detailed artifacts and sources.
bullets: Read the Engineering practice and automation handout and book Chapters 24–26.
Model training recipes and predictions about future product performance are outside this lesson.
notes: Revisit the outcomes and ask the room to state a limitation of the strongest result discussed today. A complete answer identifies a model boundary, an assumption, a missing oracle or the scope of the underlying evidence.
Assign the detailed reading to the relevant chapters. The omitted topics are explicit scope boundaries, not claims that those topics are unimportant.
